sentences.text: Parksosaurus was a small, bipedal, herbivorous dinosaur known from a partially articulated skeleton and partial skull.
Parksosaurus warreni is the only known species in the extinct genus Parksosaurus.
This animal was a small, bipedal, running dinosaur.
It possessed short but strong forelimbs and long, powerful hind limbs.
The dinosaur possessed a strong beak.
Parksosaurus measured approximately 2.5 meters in length.
Its body featured thin, partly ossified cartilaginous plates along its ribs, similar to Thescelosaurus.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated Parksosaurus weighed 45 kilograms.
The holotype skeleton of Parksosaurus was discovered in 1922 by a University of Toronto expedition in Alberta, Canada.
Professor William A. Parks first described the species in 1926, initially naming it Thescelosaurus warreni.
Paleontologist William Parks described the specimen ROM 804 in 1926.
Charles Mortram Sternberg established the genus Parksosaurus in 1937 to separate it from Thescelosaurus.
The fossil was found approximately 0.5 miles from the Red Deer River and 100 feet above the water level near Rumsey Ferry.
Parksosaurus received a redescription in 1973.
Parksosaurus was likely a small, swift bipedal herbivore in life.
In life, Parksosaurus was likely a small, fast, bipedal herbivore.
Researchers suggest that Parksosaurus had long toes adapted for walking on mud near rivers and strong forelimbs used for burrowing.
In 2010, Paul suggested that Parksosaurus's long toes were an adaptation for walking on mud or clay near rivers.
Paul also suggested that Parksosaurus's strong arms were used for digging.
Parksosaurus is classified within the family Thescelosauridae.
The species belongs to the subfamily Thescelosaurinae.
Parksosaurus is a member of the dinosaur family Thescelosauridae.
The parent group of Parksosaurus is Thescelosaurinae.
Charles M. Sternberg assigned Parksosaurus to the subfamily Hypsilophodontinae alongside Hypsilophodon and Dysalotosaurus.
In 2008, Richard Butler and colleagues placed Parksosaurus near the South American genus Gasparinisaura.
Parksosaurus lived around 70 million years ago during the early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Fossils of Parksosaurus date to approximately 69.5 million years ago from the base of Unit 4 of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation.
Parksosaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 70 million years ago in the Maastrichtian stage.
Parksosaurus fossils have been found in what is now North America.
Parksosaurus lived between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian.
Parksosaurus is known from the base of Unit 4 of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation, dating to approximately 69.5 million years ago.
The habitat of Parksosaurus was influenced by the encroaching Western Interior Seaway, a shallow sea covering mid-North America.
The Horseshoe Canyon Formation is interpreted to have had significant marine influence.

There is debate regarding the exact placement of Parksosaurus, with some studies suggesting it is the sister taxon to Thescelosaurus while others suggest it may be close to the South American genus Gasparinisaura.
The phylogeny of basal ornithopods is poorly known and remains under study.
